1.pericope_label: Jesus before Pilate, the accusations, and the first acquittal

schools.summary: Gill describes the whole company rising and the priests' refusal of the verdict; Calvin gives the reason for the trial itself, that since Christ came to bear the punishment of our sins it was proper he should first be condemned by the mouth of his judge.
Henry follows the Sanhedrin's change of course when they found they could go no further in their own court, and traces the accusations one by one as falsely framed.

Clarke calls the charges the falsest slanders that could be invented, disproved by our Lord's whole conduct, records the addition in several copies of the Itala about destroying the law and the prophets, and observes that neither Christ nor any follower ever forbade constitutional taxes to a lawful prince; Wesley notes that Pilate's verdict followed a hearing.

Robertson counts three charges and notes that none gives the real reason nor mentions the Sanhedrin's own condemnation, since they no longer held the power of life and death, calls the charge about tribute a flat untruth after their failure to trap him, explains why the word king compelled Pilate where Christ would not, and refers the missing examination to John's account; Ellicott finds Luke's report more definite than the other Gospels, traces the charge to the earlier question about tribute, and notes that the Greek enlarges it from the poll-tax to taxes generally; Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic phrase about corrupting one's food publicly and the Talmudic sentence naming Jesus, which the Aruch cites with Jeroboam instead; Barnes explains the acquittal.

Augustine explains that Luke went back over the morning and set down the charges the other evangelists omit, and reads the answer to Pilate as deliberately the same words used to the chief priests so that the governor might be condemned out of his own mouth; Bede sees the delivery to the Gentiles as a fulfilment of prophecy, suggests that Pilate had heard the saying about rendering to Caesar and so set that charge aside as a palpable lie, and answers that the accusers convict themselves; Tertullian holds that Jesus answered as before so as not to seem driven by fear into saying more, and distributes the second psalm among Pilate, the tribes of Israel, Herod and the chief priests.

Theophylact answers the charge of forbidding tribute by observing that Christ commanded it paid and fled when the multitude would have crowned him, hears derision in Pilate's question to a poor and naked man accused of seeking a kingdom, and explains the renewed clamour as the resort of men who had nothing else to support their calumny, Galilee being named on purpose to alarm a governor who knew the Galileans to be seditious; Cyril of Jerusalem bids us not be ashamed of the Cross.
Cyril of Alexandria's comment at this point still stands on the night trial and the mocking of the previous chapter, over which he sets Jeremiah's wish for waters on his head and a fountain of tears.

debates: Why Pilate asked only about the kingship: Bede supposes he had heard the saying about rendering to Caesar and dismissed the tribute charge as a lie, while Theophylact hears mockery of the whole indictment in the question
outliers: Lightfoot traces the first accusation to a rabbinic idiom for corrupting doctrine, and reports that the Talmudic instance names Jesus of Nazareth where a later authority substitutes Jeroboam

6.pericope_label: Jesus sent to Herod, the silence, the mocking, and the reconciliation of the rulers

schools.summary: Gill notes that Galilee lay under Herod and that the questioning got nothing; Calvin turns Herod's gladness into a portrait of the flesh which would see God in his works without submitting to his authority, observes that he chose to have Christ at his feet as a malefactor rather than receive him as a teacher, finds it inevitable that a haughty man should despise one of contemptible appearance while allowing the pride no excuse, holds that God purposely hardened him by the spectacle, and notes that the whole retinue is named because the honour due to God is seldom rendered in the courts of kings.
Henry recalls how much Herod had heard of Jesus in Galilee and how long he had wished to see him.

Clarke argues that the robe was white, as the Jewish nobility wore, so that Herod mocked after his own country's custom where the Roman soldiers used purple, citing Bishop Pearce, and warns that the modern conjectures about the rulers' old quarrel should be taken as no more than guesses; Wesley guesses that Herod's questions concerned the miracles.

Ellicott explains Pilate's motive as an attempt to shift responsibility for condemning one he believed innocent, describes the court Herod kept at the Passover with his rabbis and troops after long seclusion, and suggests that this incident, peculiar to Luke, reached him through Manaen or others of the Herodian household; Lightfoot asks whether a capital jurisdiction was being conceded and answers that Pilate acted to flatter Herod or to shed the odium, and would render the robe white and shining but for Luke's express phrase elsewhere, taking it for a fool's coat; Barnes and Robertson give the jurisdiction, the exceeding joy and the vehement accusing, and Barnes denies that the two rulers were united in hating Jesus, since Pilate wished to release him.

Bede reads Pilate's question as relief at an opening to escape sentence and prefers that the tetrarch of Christ's own country should judge him, and reads the new alliance as a figure of Gentiles and Jews agreeing to persecute Christians; Gregory says Herod wished to make proof of Christ's fame and adds that the Redeemer, questioned, held his peace and, expected, disdained to work miracles, choosing to be set at nought by the proud rather than praised by the hollow; Ambrose explains the silence by Herod's unbelief and the Lord's shunning of display, draws a rule for teachers whose hearers praise without amending, and takes the two rulers for a type of Israel and the Gentiles reconciled through the Passion.
Cyril of Jerusalem sets the sending under the prophecy that they should carry him bound as a present to a king, and meets the objection that Pilate was no king.

debates: What the friendship of Herod and Pilate signifies: Ambrose makes it a type of Jew and Gentile reconciled by the Passion, Bede the contrary figure of both agreeing to persecute Christians, and Barnes denies any such union, holding that Pilate wished to release Jesus and both merely made sport of him
What the robe was: Clarke and Lightfoot both argue for white rather than purple, Lightfoot taking it for a fool's coat and inferring that Herod thought Jesus deranged
outliers: Ellicott traces this episode, which no other evangelist reports, to Luke's contact with Manaen or others of the Herodian household
Ambrose turns the silence before Herod into a rule for teachers, that we should be wholly silent to hearers who praise what they hear and never follow it

13.pericope_label: Pilate's second acquittal, the offer to scourge, and the release of Barabbas

schools.summary: Gill follows the repetition of the charge, the record of Barabbas and the final exchange; Calvin calls it plain injustice to punish one already declared free from all blame, explains it by the habit of earthly men who commit small injuries under compulsion and then claim the praise of mildness, argues that a scourged and dismissed Christ would have carried shame without advantage to our salvation where on the cross he triumphed as in a chariot, and turns the scene on his own age by charging those who make the faithful deny the gospel to save their lives.

Henry presses the inconsistency, that if Pilate believed him innocent he ought to have released him at once, and follows the governor's shifts down to the delivering of Jesus to the will of those who hated him.

Clarke finds the accusations frivolous to the last degree, explains why Herod of all men could judge whether sedition had been raised in Galilee, records the variant which makes Herod send him back rather than Pilate send them to him, prefers nothing worthy of death committed by him to done unto him on the authority of Attic usage, and notes the third protest of innocence; Wesley marks the proposal to chastise as the point where Pilate begins to give way.

Robertson notes the calling together of rulers and people, the shouting, the pressing with loud voices and the formal sentence; Barnes finds it hard to see why a man who believed Jesus innocent should propose to whip him, since that was as unjust as crucifixion, supposes he hoped to conciliate the accusers by a spectacle of disgrace, and cites the Roman practice of a slight punishment where a grave charge was not made out; Ellicott traces the word for chastisement from the correction of children to the Roman scourge, finds Pilate halting between two opinions, weighs whether the verse on the custom belongs to the text, and observes that Luke alone gives the ground of Barabbas's imprisonment.

Augustine explains that Luke resumes the business before the governor after the digression and has omitted Pilate's question to our Lord; Ambrose states the paradox that the judge who acquits Christ is made the minister of his crucifixion, finds it fitting that men demanding the death of the innocent should ask pardon for a murderer since what innocence hates guilt loves, and presses the meaning of the name Barabbas as son of a father, so that those told they were of their father the devil prefer the son of their father to the true Son of God.

Theophylact makes the double acquittal a legal point, that by the testimony of two men Jesus is declared innocent while his accusers produce no credible witness, so that truth triumphs when the accused is silent and his enemies witness for him; Cyril of Jerusalem takes the passage as ground for glorying in the Cross.
Cyril of Alexandria's homily at this point still runs on the accusations and the demand for Barabbas rather than on the sentence itself.

debates: Why Pilate proposed to scourge a man he had declared innocent: Barnes supposes he hoped a spectacle of disgrace would satisfy the accusers and cites the Roman practice for unproved charges, Ellicott sees a man halting between two opinions, and Calvin calls it simple injustice dressed as mildness
Whether the verse on the custom of releasing a prisoner belongs to the text, which Ellicott weighs
outliers: Ambrose reads the name Barabbas etymologically and makes the crowd's choice a figure of preferring the son of their father to the true Son of God
Calvin turns the scourging into a charge against the judges of his own day who spare men's lives by making them deny the gospel

26.pericope_label: Simon of Cyrene, and the word to the daughters of Jerusalem

schools.summary: Gill keeps to the plain account of the pressing of Simon and refers the coming woes to the siege, reading the green tree of Christ and the dry of the nation; Calvin allows that some still lamented though the whole people had joined in the fury, denies that the women are reproved for weeping without cause and takes the words as a warning of far greater cause to come, finds in them proof of the fortitude with which Christ advanced to death and of the Father's care for him when all thought him forsaken, and makes the proverb confirm that God would never have permitted such a death but for an expiation of the world's sins.

Henry distinguishes the mourners who followed from those who clamoured, treats the lament of the daughters of Jerusalem as sincere but misdirected, and allows the cry to the mountains a further reach in the damnation of sinners beyond the siege.

Clarke uses the words to correct devout persons distressed at being unable to weep over the Passion, holding that no human spirit can share sufferings only God manifest in the flesh could bear and that they are matter not of sorrow but of rejoicing, names the legend of the stigmata and the hymns that ask for one drop of the cup, and reverses the proverb of the trees, that if men spare not a tree worth preserving the withered one will surely be cut down; Wesley refers the cry to the siege and reads the green tree of Christ.

Barnes gives the parallel in Matthew, explains the beatitude on the barren as an inversion of a Jewish mother's hope, and expounds the proverb both of the Roman destruction and of the sufferings of the wicked hereafter, an innocent sufferer having neither remorse nor eternity against him; Ellicott takes the women's mourning for genuine grief and keeps the historical reference throughout; Robertson notes the imperfect of the following crowd and calls the beatitude one turned upside down; Lightfoot carries the cry to the mountains into the Apocalypse and infers that the chapter concerns the plagues before the fall of Jerusalem, adding that this may help in discovering that book's method.

The Gloss marks the transition from condemnation to crucifixion and preserves the harmonising of John's account with the Synoptists, that Christ carried the cross out of the city and Simon the rest of the way; Bede reads the names, that Simon means obedient and Cyrene an heir, so that the man denotes the Gentiles once aliens to the covenant and now made heirs by obedience, bearing the cross as they forsake the pagan rites.

Theophylact explains that no one else would carry the wood, counted an abomination, so that it was laid on Simon to his dishonour, yet finds in it the fulfilment of the prophecy that the government should be upon his shoulder, the cross being Christ's government and worn as a mark of dignity, and concludes that Christ reigns in us only by hardships, which is why the luxurious are enemies of his cross.

debates: Whether the women are reproved for weeping: Calvin denies it and takes the words as a warning of greater cause to come, while Clarke uses them to deny that any man can share the Passion at all

How far the cry to the mountains reaches: Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott and Wesley refer it to the siege, Henry allows it a further reach in the judgment of sinners, and Lightfoot carries it into the Apocalypse
How the proverb of the green tree runs: Barnes makes the green tree hard to kindle and the dry easy, Clarke makes it a tree worth preserving against one fit only for felling
outliers: Clarke turns the verse into a rebuke of hymns and legends that ask to share Christ's agonies, answering that one drop of that cup would bear a soul down to endless ruin
Lightfoot uses the parallel with the Apocalypse to argue for the date and method of that book

32.pericope_label: The two malefactors, the place of a skull, and the crucifixion

schools.summary: Gill identifies the two as malefactors and describes the manner of the crucifying and the position between them.

Henry finds in the company the fulfilment of the word that he was numbered with the transgressors and adds that he was ranked among them and not merely treated as one, describes the nailing to the cross as it lay upon the ground, and marvels that such barbarity was shown to one against whom nothing was proved.
Clarke presses the Greek to show that Luke does not reckon Jesus another malefactor of the same kind but distinguishes him, and takes Calvary simply as the skull.

Barnes and Robertson give the leading out and the crucifying, Robertson noting the imperfect and the sense of the word for skull; Ellicott explains that the English name comes through the Latin, that the Greek gives no ground for the popular picture of a hill, weighs the competing accounts of how the place was named and prefers the shape or use of the ground to any legend, and observes that Luke alone records the malefactors being led out with him from the first.

Bede explains the name from the places outside the gate where condemned criminals were beheaded, draws the moral that the innocent was crucified among the guilty so that where sin abounded grace might much more abound, and reads the two robbers as those who under the faith of Christ undergo martyrdom or a stricter continence, the one for eternal glory imitating the thief on the right and the one who seeks men's praise the thief on the left.
Cyril of Jerusalem takes the whole scene as the ground of the Church's glorying in the Cross.

Athanasius reports the Jewish opinion that Calvary was Adam's burial place, and defends this particular death at length: that Christ came to accomplish man's death and not his own, that he could neither die of sickness nor die in secret since death must precede resurrection, that a more glorious end would have left him suspected of lacking power over every death, that the cross was chosen as the most shameful so that in destroying it the dominion of death might be overthrown, and that the body was kept entire lest it become an excuse to those who would divide the Church; Gregory of Nyssa takes the cross branching from one centre into four terminations for the power and providence of him who hung on it reaching everywhere, and his block carries the further reading of the four dimensions and the note that the thieves were set beside him to share his reproach though it did not so turn out; Cyril of Alexandria states the rule that the only-begotten did not suffer in the nature in which he is God but in his earthly nature.

debates: Why the place was called the skull: Athanasius reports the tradition that Adam was buried there, Bede explains it from the beheading of criminals outside the gate, and Ellicott prefers the shape or use of the ground to any legend
Whether Luke's phrase ranks Jesus with the malefactors, which Clarke denies on grammatical grounds
outliers: Athanasius answers the objection that Christ might have chosen a more glorious death by arguing that any other end would have left his power over death in doubt
Cyril of Alexandria's homily at this point is still running on the sentence and the daughters of Jerusalem rather than on the crucifixion

34.pericope_label: The prayer for the crucifiers, and the parting of the garments

schools.summary: Gill sets the prayer first among the words from the cross and takes the parting of the raiment as the exact fulfilment of the psalm; Calvin finds in the words the proof that Christ was the lamb led out to be sacrificed, since he not only abstained from revenge but pleaded for the salvation of those who tormented him, and notes that Peter proposes this very forbearance as the pattern of our patience.
Clarke weighs how far ignorance excuses and observes that the soldiers acted by custom rather than malice; Wesley observes that our Lord passed most of his time on the cross in prayer.

Barnes takes the prayer for a fulfilment of the prophecy of intercession for transgressors and applies it to Romans and Jews together, the soldiers being ignorant that he was the Son of God and the Jews not knowing what judgments they were bringing on their country; Ellicott narrows it to the soldiers who nailed him, since Pilate knew he had condemned the innocent and the priests sinned against light, while allowing an ultimate extension to all who sin without knowing; Robertson agrees that the prayer was for the soldiers and not the Sanhedrin and adds that some of the oldest documents omit the verse though the words are utterly unlike anyone else; Lightfoot reports the rabbinic tradition that Moses ministered in a seamless white vestment and records with contempt the reason given for its seamlessness.

Ambrose considers the condition in which Christ ascends the cross, that he sees him naked, and draws the lesson that whoever would overcome the world should seek none of its appliances, since Adam was overcome seeking a covering while Christ overcame by laying his aside; he adds that in putting off the royal garments he showed that he suffered not as God but as man, and his block carries the further reading that he wore our garments, the signs of Adam's death, to put them off and clothe us with incorruption.

Chrysostom sets the prayer against the Lord's own command to pray for persecutors, holds that he prayed not from inability to pardon but to teach us to do so in deed as well as word, and limits the petition to forgiveness upon repentance; the catena adds that he obtained the fruit of his prayer in those who believed after the Passion, that he prayed for such as had zeal without knowledge and not for those who chose to crucify rather than confess him, and that those who remained in unbelief afterwards cannot plead ignorance; Theophylact asks what the soldiers wanted with such clothes and answers that they were in want, or rather acted from reproach and wantonness.

debates: For whom the prayer was offered: Barnes takes in both Romans and Jews, Ellicott and Robertson restrict it to the soldiers and exclude the Sanhedrin, and Chrysostom makes it conditional upon repentance
Whether the verse belongs to the text, which Robertson doubts on manuscript grounds while holding the words certainly authentic
outliers: Lightfoot pursues the seamless coat into rabbinic tradition about Moses' vestment of consecration, and dismisses the reason given there for its lack of seams
The catena preserves a note that the casting of lots commends the grace of God, since a lot yields not to merit but to the secret judgment of God

35.pericope_label: The mocking of rulers and soldiers, and the superscription

schools.summary: Gill sets out the standing and beholding, takes the soldiers' words as a taunt drawn from the title over his head, and reports its wording.

Clarke calls the derision the utmost contempt, refers the vinegar and the superscription to the fuller accounts in the other Gospels, and describes the three languages of the inscription; Wesley marks the parallel between the rulers' challenge to the Christ and the soldiers' to the king of the Jews.

Ellicott notes that Luke uses the generic term for the Sanhedrin where Matthew particularises, that the verb for derision implies the curled lip of scorn, that the taunt about saving others was an unconscious prophecy like Caiaphas's, and that this is the only place in the New Testament where the adjective chosen is applied directly to Christ, and reads the offer of vinegar as touched with some rough kindliness; Lightfoot shows that vinegar was the common drink of Roman soldiers, cites the discipline forbidding wine on campaign and the provisioning of frontier cities, and reconciles the evangelists by supposing two or even three cups; Barnes and Robertson give the tenses and the history of the inscription.

Ambrose finds the title rightly placed above the cross, since Christ's kingdom is not of the human body but of the power of God, and reads it beside the sayings that his kingdom is not of this world and that the Word was God; his block runs on to the penitent thief, where he takes the exchange as a remarkable example of conversion, the Lord pardoning quickly because the thief is quickly converted and grace being more abundant than prayer, since he asked to be remembered and was answered with paradise; Gregory observes that nothing remained free from torture but heart and tongue, so that the thief offered God the whole of what he found free, and finds all three of the Apostle's virtues in him at once.

Theophylact sees the devil's device turned a second time against himself in an accusation published in three characters, and presses the choice of tongues, that the most powerful of nations, the wisest, and those who most worshipped God were signified to be subject to Christ; his block adds the figure of a king carrying the best of his spoils in triumph, the Lord having despoiled the devil of part of his plunder; Chrysostom makes the condemned thief perform the office of judge and distinguishes the confession that precedes punishment from the confession made to salvation.
Gregory of Nyssa's block at this key turns to the penitent thief rather than to the title.

debates: How many cups were offered and by whom, Lightfoot proposing two or three to reconcile the wine mingled with myrrh, the vinegar mingled with gall, and the soldiers' plain vinegar
Whether the soldiers' offer was pure mockery, which Ellicott doubts, allowing a touch of rough kindliness
outliers: The catena blocks keyed at the superscription in fact expound the penitent thief, so that the fathers' comment on verses thirty-nine to forty-three stands filed here
Ellicott observes that the mockers' word chosen is the only direct application of that adjective to Christ in the New Testament

39.pericope_label: The two malefactors, and the promise of paradise

schools.summary: Gill presses the question whether a man so near death should not fear God, defines paradise as the place where the souls of the righteous wait, and notes that Jesus answered immediately; Calvin observes that the reproach from a fellow-sufferer completed Christ's abasement, and calls the penitent thief's faith the most remarkable example since the creation of the world, wondering that a murderer untaught in Christ's school should rise higher than the apostles, adoring as king one who hung on a gallows, asking what marks of royalty he could have seen, answering that he beheld life in death and glory in shame, turning the example against his readers' sloth, and tracing his assurance of pardon to his seeing in that death a sacrifice able to expiate the world's sins.

Clarke takes the rebuke as evidence that suffering had wrought on one and not the other, reports that Marcion and the Manichees omitted the verse of promise, takes the saying for a strong proof of the soul's immateriality, and attacks the expedient of placing a comma after today so as to make the sense I tell thee this today, calling it a feeble criticism a good cause cannot need; Wesley marks the change from the plural of the other evangelists to the singular and defines paradise as the place where souls wait.

Barnes opens with the discrepancy between Matthew and Luke over the thieves, reads the impenitent man's prayer as a request to be spared the cross rather than his sins and compares those who pray in sickness and forget on recovery, glosses the due reward of their deeds, doubts that the day can be pushed forward to the resurrection, and notes that the promise is peculiar to Luke; Ellicott collects and then sets aside the legends of Dysmas who had once attacked the holy family, finds the penitent impressed by the sufferer's holiness so that words uttered in mockery worked his conversion, locates the root in a fear of God his companion lacked, observes that accepting his punishment as just made it reformatory rather than penal, and traces the word paradise from a Persian term for a royal park through the Greek translators; Robertson marks the imperfect of the railing and gives the plain construction of the promise; Lightfoot shows from rabbinic usage that paradise meant the garden of Eden and reports the tradition of the four who entered it.

Leo, following the Passion through a course of sermons, finds in the two robbers the difference that must be made among all men displayed in the very incidents of the cross, the believing thief a type of those to be saved and the blasphemer a figure of those to be damned.
Cyril of Jerusalem addresses the robber directly, asking what power led him to so great a confession.

debates: Whether the promise means paradise the same day or a declaration made that day, Clarke attacking the comma that produces the second sense
How far the legends of the penitent thief may be used: Ellicott reports them fully and then confines himself to what Luke records
Whether the impenitent thief's cry was a prayer at all, which Barnes denies since he asked only to be spared the cross
outliers: Clarke reports that Marcion and the Manichees are said to have struck the verse of promise from their copies
Calvin sets the thief's faith above that of all the apostles and makes it the chief marvel of the chapter

44.pericope_label: The darkness, the rending of the veil, and the commending of the spirit

schools.summary: Gill keeps to the history of the sixth hour and the three hours' darkness.

Henry sets the passage under three heads, treats the darkness as a mourning of nature and a sign that the Sun of righteousness was withdrawing, observes that it lasted three hours and not three days as in Egypt, reads the loud cry as showing that the agony of his soul was over, and takes the commending of the spirit as a surrender into the Father's hand to be received into paradise.
Clarke and Wesley refer the discussion of the darkness to the parallel accounts in the other Gospels and keep to the plain history.
Barnes gives the hour and the extent of the darkness.

Ambrose reads the darkness morally, that the sun is eclipsed to the sacrilegious so as to overshadow their wickedness and that unbelieving eyes are darkened so that the light of faith might rise, takes the rent veil for the division of the two peoples and the profanation of the synagogue, finds in the loud cry the proof that Christ could lay down his life and take it again while distinguishing what a man sends forth from what he loses, and closes on the reach of the commended Spirit, which gives light even to the parts beneath the earth; Bede notices that Luke joins the rending of the veil to the darkness where Matthew and Mark place it at the death and concludes that he relates it by anticipation, and reads the address to the Father as declaring the Son of God and the commending as confidence rather than weakness.

Theophylact takes the rending to mean that the Holy of Holies should be inaccessible no longer but given over to the Romans and defiled, and elsewhere that the veil of enmity and sin which kept us from the holy things in heaven is broken through; Chrysostom draws from the words that the souls of the saints are no longer shut up below but are with God, Christ being the beginning of that change, and his block adds that he commends all mankind to the Father through himself since we are his members.

Cyril of Alexandria reads the darkness as the world bewailing its rightful Master and a token that the crucifiers' souls would suffer darkness, and his block preserves the argument that no common eclipse can fall at Passover full moon together with the Heliopolis observation of the moon meeting the sun out of season; Gregory of Nyssa raises the question how the Lord is at once in the heart of the earth, in paradise and in the Father's hands, answers that he who is everywhere by divine power is present in any place, and offers the further explanation that his divinity separated soul from body of its own accord while abiding in each; John Damascene states the same distribution exactly, that in respect of his body he was in the grave, in respect of his soul in hell, and with the thief in paradise.

debates: Whether Luke's placing of the rent veil before the death is out of order, which Bede resolves by anticipation
How the three sayings from the cross can be reconciled, Gregory of Nyssa answering from the omnipresence of the divine power and John Damascene by distinguishing body, soul and person
outliers: The catena preserves an eyewitness report of an eclipse seen at Heliopolis, in which the obscuration began from the east and light was lost and restored from opposite sides of the sun's diameter
Cyril of Alexandria's second block at this key is his homily on the crucifixion and the thieves, so the catena's comment here runs a pericope behind the text

45.pericope_label: The last cry, the centurion's confession, and the watchers

schools.summary: Gill refers the cause of the darkness to fuller discussions elsewhere, keeps to the record of the centurion's words, remarks that the crowd's change of temper was short-lived, and notes that the acquaintance stood as near as they durst.

Clarke refers the darkness to his examination elsewhere, observes that the last words were spoken in the confidence of one committing a trust rather than yielding to necessity, and grants that all were deeply affected while doubting how deep the impression went; Wesley keeps to the plain statement, distinguishes those who had been actors in the crime from those who came only to look, and notes that the women were witnesses of everything done.

Robertson prefers the reading of the best manuscripts, that the sun's light failed, notes that Jesus dies with a psalm on his lips, that the imperfect shows the centurion kept on glorifying God, and that the crowd went away in another temper; Barnes observes that the loud voice showed his strength unspent and explains the confession as far as a Roman soldier could have meant it; Ellicott adds that the words were the evening prayer of every Jewish child so that he died as a child falls asleep, explains the word for the sight as one used of a gathered spectacle, notes that the acquaintance standing afar off is peculiar to Luke and echoes the psalm about friend and neighbour put far away, and identifies the women with those named in the next chapter.

Augustine explains the centurion's marvel from the manner of the death, since crucified men commonly died by a lingering end while this one cried aloud and immediately expired, and then harmonises the accounts at length, showing that Matthew's earthquake and Luke's what was done are not at variance, offering two solutions for the difference between the Son of God and a righteous man, and observing that in being greatly afraid the man glorified God; Ambrose bursts out upon the breasts of the Jews harder than the rocks, since judge, officer, traitor and elements all bear witness while that hardness alone remains immovable, and makes the centurion's faith the faith of the Church confessing the Son of God in the synagogue's silence.

Theophylact finds the promise fulfilled that being lifted up he would draw all men, since from the cross he drew the thief, the centurion and some of the people, and reads the hour as the beginning of the drawing of the nations; Cyril of Jerusalem takes the darkness and the death together as the ground of the Church's confession.

debates: Whether the centurion said the Son of God or a righteous man, and what he meant by it, which Augustine settles either by allowing both sayings or by making Luke give the sense the soldier intended
What the smiting of the breasts signified, the catena offering both grief for one unjustly slain and terror at having demanded his death
outliers: Ambrose sets the acquittal by the judge, the belief of the officer, the self-condemnation of the traitor and the shaking of the elements against the unmoved hardness of the Jews
The catena contrasts the Gentiles who glorified God by open confession with those who struck their breasts and went home silent

50.pericope_label: Joseph of Arimathea, the burial, and the sabbath rest

schools.summary: Gill notes that Joseph was a disciple though secretly, that he had not consented to the council, and that the women marked the tomb and how the body was laid.

Henry closes the chapter on the burial as the last stage of Christ's humiliation, and takes the women's resting according to the commandment as a sign that the sabbath was still binding, though the day was afterwards altered.

Clarke explains the preparation as the day before the sabbath, discusses the custom of embalming and how far the Jews practised it, and refers the reader to his fuller notes elsewhere; Wesley remarks that a good and just man was found even in that council.

Barnes gives the taking down, the winding in linen and the women's observation of the tomb; Ellicott explains that the phrase about the counsel and deed clears Joseph of both the decision and its execution, treats the preparation and the sabbath rest at length, and notes that Luke alone follows the women so closely through these hours; Robertson marks the double negative, the formal request for the body and the reckoning of the day of preparation; Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic background, that shrouds for the executed were made from worn wrappings of the Law to their disgrace, explains the principle that shameful handling was thought to increase a condemned man's atonement, applies the same rule to the withholding of lamentation, examines the phrase that the sabbath drew on and offers both the sabbath candles and the Jewish use of light for evening, and reasons about the interval called between the suns in which the women could buy their spices.

Bede explains the office of a decurio, identifies Arimathea with the Ramathaim of Elkanah and Samuel, finds Joseph fitted by his righteousness and worthy by his rank to obtain the body, and draws from the simplicity of the burial a rebuke of rich men who cannot be without their wealth even in their graves; the Greek Exposition explains that a secret disciple burst the bonds of fear and gained a precious jewel by the meekness of his asking; Augustine states the difficulty that one who was a disciple in secret dared what open followers did not, and answers from the confidence of his rank and his readiness on this occasion to disregard Jewish hostility; Ambrose turns to the mystical sense, that the just man buries the body of Christ and covers it with linen, and bids the reader clothe that body with its own glory so as to become just.

Theophylact reads the spices as a measure of the women's faith, that not yet believing enough they prepared ointments as for a mere man after the Jewish manner, and observes that they worked until sunset and then kept the commanded rest from evening to evening.

debates: Why a secret disciple dared what open followers did not, which Augustine answers from the confidence of his rank and the Greek Exposition from a sudden growth of zeal
What the women's spices show: Theophylact takes them for a defect of faith, while the moderns treat them simply as the customary office to the dead
outliers: Lightfoot explains the Jewish rule that a condemned man was wrapped in worn and dirty cloths because shameful treatment was thought to increase his atonement, and notes how differently Christ's word to the women must be understood
Bede turns the plainness of Christ's burial into a rebuke of the rich who carry their wealth into the grave
